facts.text: Voltage (V, in volts) is the electrical potential difference between two points; it must always be measured between a point and a defined reference, never 'at' a single point in isolation.
Current (I, in amperes) is the flow of charge through a conductor; it is measured in series with the load, not in parallel across it.

Resistance (R, in ohms) is opposition to DC current; it is measured with the circuit unpowered, and large capacitors should be safely discharged before measuring to avoid both false readings and meter damage.
Power (P, in watts) equals voltage times current: P = V * I. Combined with Ohm's law this also gives P = I^2 * R and P = V^2 / R for purely resistive loads.
Ohm's law for a linear resistor: V = I * R, I = V / R, R = V / I. It applies only to resistive elements at a given temperature; semiconductor junctions and active regulators do not obey it directly.

A resistance-to-ground reading on a power rail that is significantly lower than the known normal for that board suggests a short or low-impedance path on that rail; a reading near zero ohms on a main power rail is a strong indicator of a hard short, but a soft short can still allow partial operation.
Kirchhoff's current law (KCL): the algebraic sum of currents entering a node equals the sum leaving; charge is conserved at every node.
Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL): the algebraic sum of voltages around any closed loop is zero; this is the basis for analyzing series power paths and voltage drops across protection devices.
Resistors in series add directly: R_total = R1 + R2 + ... ; the same current flows through each, and voltage divides in proportion to resistance.
Resistors in parallel combine as 1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ... ; the same voltage appears across each, and the total is always less than the smallest individual resistance.

An ideal capacitor blocks DC and passes AC; in a DC power rail it stores charge, filters ripple, and provides transient current. A shorted capacitor on a power rail is a common cause of a low-resistance-to-ground fault.

An inductor resists changes in current and is used in switching regulators as the energy-storage element; its DC resistance is normally very low (milliohms to a few ohms) and should not be mistaken for a short.

Bulk capacitors on power rails can hold charge after power is removed; always discharge them (with an appropriate bleed resistor, not a screwdriver) before measuring resistance or probing, to avoid both false readings and meter or finger injury.
A diode conducts current from anode to cathode when forward-biased (anode ~0.6-0.7 V above cathode for silicon) and blocks when reverse-biased, until its reverse breakdown voltage.
A Zener diode is operated in reverse breakdown to provide a stable reference voltage; its nominal Zener voltage is component-specific and must be read from the datasheet, not assumed.

An N-channel enhancement MOSFET turns on when its gate-source voltage exceeds its threshold (Vgs(th)); current then flows from drain to source. P-channel turns on when Vgs is negative of the required magnitude.

On laptop motherboards the main input (adapter) MOSFET is usually a P-channel or back-to-back N-channel arrangement used as an ideal diode / load switch; a failed input MOSFET can pass no voltage, leak current, or pass voltage in both directions.

A MOSFET can fail short (gate-oxide punch-through or drain-source avalanche) so the rail is always connected, or fail open (bond wire or channel damage) so no current passes; both modes appear in repair experience.

A bipolar junction transistor (BJT) is a current-controlled device: a small base current controls a larger collector current. NPN conducts when base is ~0.7 V above emitter; PNP when base is ~0.7 V below emitter.

In switching service a BJT is driven hard into saturation; in linear service (small-signal amplifiers, bias networks) it operates in the forward-active region. The intended mode must be known before judging a measurement.
An operational amplifier with negative feedback holds its inverting input at the same potential as the non-inverting input (virtual short); the output moves to whatever value makes this true.

A comparator has no feedback (or only positive feedback) and its output saturates to one rail or the other based on which input is higher; it is used to assert power-good, over-current, or under-voltage flags.
